title: Lightning Messages: The Electric Telegraph
summary: In the 1830s and 1840s, inventors in Britain and America finally made electricity carry messages along a wire. Little needles twitched, keys clicked, and the news that once took days by horse now arrived in a blink. Soon wires followed the railways across whole countries.

sections.heading: A Race on Two Sides of the Ocean
paragraphs: By the 1830s, scientists knew three exciting things. A battery could push a steady electric current through a wire. That current could make a compass needle swing. And a coil of wire wrapped around iron became a magnet whenever electricity flowed through it. Put those clues together and a thrilling question appears: if you switch a current on and off at one end of a long wire, could someone at the other end see or hear it, and read a message?

Many people tried to answer that question at almost the same time. In Russia, the diplomat Pavel Schilling built a needle telegraph in the early 1830s. In the German town of Göttingen, the famous mathematician Carl Friedrich Gauss and the physicist Wilhelm Weber strung a wire about a kilometre long over the rooftops in 1833 so they could signal between the observatory and the physics laboratory. None of these became a big public system, but they proved the idea could work.

The two names that history remembers most are from Britain and the United States. In London, a businessman named William Fothergill Cooke teamed up with a scientist named Charles Wheatstone. In New York, a painter named Samuel Morse worked with a young mechanic named Alfred Vail and several helpers. Each team built a different kind of telegraph, and each one changed its country. So when people ask who invented the electric telegraph, the honest answer is: quite a few people, building on each other's discoveries, racing in different places at the same time.

The word telegraph comes from Greek words meaning far writing. The Chappe brothers had already used it for their tower-and-arm system in France. Now the far writing was going to be done by electricity, and electricity moves along a wire so fast that, for a message travelling between two cities, the delay is far too small for any person to notice.

sections.heading: Five Needles, a Railway and a Famous Arrest
paragraphs: William Cooke was not a scientist at first. He had been an officer in the army in India and was studying medicine in Germany when, in 1836, he saw a professor at Heidelberg demonstrate an electric needle telegraph based on Schilling's work. He hurried back to England full of plans. He soon realised he needed help with the science, so in 1837 he went to see Charles Wheatstone, a professor at King's College London who was already experimenting with sending electric signals through long wires. Wheatstone was a clever, shy man who also invented a small musical instrument called the concertina and an early 3D viewer called the stereoscope.

Their two personalities did not always get along, and later they argued bitterly over who deserved more credit. But together they received a British patent in 1837 for a needle telegraph. Picture a wooden board shaped like a diamond, with the letters of the alphabet painted on it in a grid. Across the middle of the board stand five magnetic needles, each one able to swing left or right. When the operator at the far end pressed certain buttons, electric current flowed through two of the wires, and two needles tilted toward each other. Wherever their imaginary lines crossed, that was the letter being sent.

This design had a clever advantage: the person reading it did not need to learn any code. They just looked at which letter the needles were pointing to. But it also had a problem. Five needles could only point to 20 different letters, so C, J, Q, U, X and Z were left out. Senders had to spell creatively, using other letters that sounded similar. And the system needed five or six separate wires, which was expensive to build and maintain.

Over time, Cooke and Wheatstone made simpler versions with two needles and then just one needle. With fewer needles, the operator could no longer simply read a letter off the board. Instead, each letter became a pattern of left and right swings that operators had to memorise. The single-needle telegraph, which needed far less wire, turned out to be so reliable that some were still in use on British railways in the 1930s, almost a hundred years after the first patent.

Railways and telegraphs grew up together like twins. Railways needed a fast way to know where trains were, so that two trains would not end up on the same track heading toward each other. Telegraphs needed long, straight, guarded strips of land along which to run their wires. A railway line was perfect.

In 1838 Cooke and Wheatstone's telegraph was installed along the Great Western Railway in England, between Paddington station in London and West Drayton, about 21 kilometres (13 miles) away. It is often described as the first commercial electric telegraph in the world. Soon the line was extended to Slough, near Windsor Castle. Ordinary people could pay to send messages along it, and some came just to marvel at the machine.

The telegraph became truly famous in Britain because of a crime. On 1 January 1845, a woman was found poisoned in a house near Slough. A man in an unusual long brown coat, dressed like a Quaker, had been seen leaving and boarding a train to London. The train was much faster than any horse, so in the past he would simply have disappeared into the busy city. But this time the station staff at Slough sent a description of him by telegraph to Paddington. Because the needle telegraph had no letter Q, the message had to spell Quaker as KWAKER. When the train arrived, a police officer was waiting. He followed the man, John Tawell, who was arrested the next day and later convicted.

Newspapers everywhere reported the story. For the first time, ordinary people understood that a message could outrun a train. According to a popular story, the telegraph wires near Slough were nicknamed the cords that hanged John Tawell. After that, people began to think of the telegraph not as a strange scientific toy but as something that could change real life.

sections.heading: The Painter Who Wanted Faster News
paragraphs: Across the Atlantic, the American story begins with an artist. Samuel Finley Breese Morse was born in 1791 in Charlestown, Massachusetts. He studied painting in London and became a well-known portrait painter in the United States. He painted presidents and famous visitors, and in 1826 he helped found the National Academy of Design in New York. Science interested him too, but painting was his career.

His biographers tell a sad story from 1825. Morse was in Washington, D.C., painting a portrait of the Marquis de Lafayette, when a letter came from his father saying that his young wife, Lucretia, was very ill. By the time the slow news reached him and he travelled home to Connecticut, she had already died and been buried. Many writers think this painful experience of news arriving too late stayed with him for the rest of his life.

In 1832, Morse was sailing home from Europe on a ship called the Sully. At dinner, the passengers talked about electricity and electromagnets, and a scientist named Charles Thomas Jackson described experiments he had seen in Europe. Morse became excited by the idea that electricity could carry signals along a wire, and he began filling his sketchbook with plans. He later claimed the whole idea as his own, though Jackson disagreed, and the two men quarrelled about it for years.

Morse was a good artist but not an expert in electricity. Back in New York, where he taught painting at the university now called New York University, he got important help. Leonard Gale, a chemistry professor there, showed him how to use more powerful batteries and many turns of wire so his electromagnet would work at the end of a long line. Gale also pointed Morse to the work of the American scientist Joseph Henry, who had built some of the strongest electromagnets in the world. Henry had already shown how a weak current could switch on a second, stronger circuit. This idea, called a relay, meant a signal could be refreshed along the way, so it could travel much farther without fading away.

In 1837 a young man named Alfred Vail watched one of Morse's demonstrations. Vail was skilled with machines, and his family owned the Speedwell Ironworks in Morristown, New Jersey. He joined the project, put in money, and rebuilt Morse's clumsy prototype into a much better machine. In January 1838 the team demonstrated their telegraph at Speedwell over about 3 kilometres (2 miles) of wire coiled around a room. Morse received a US patent in 1840, but he still needed money to build a real line between two cities.

sections.heading: Dots, Dashes and a Single Wire
paragraphs: The most important idea in the American telegraph was simplicity. Instead of several wires and needles pointing at letters, Morse and Vail used just one wire, plus the ground itself to complete the circuit. At the sending end was a key, a springy metal lever. Press it down and you close the circuit, so current flows. Let it go and the circuit opens, so the current stops. That is all: on and off, on and off.

At the receiving end, the current flowed through an electromagnet. Each time current arrived, the electromagnet pulled a small iron bar called an armature toward it. In the first machines, called registers, the armature pressed a pointed stylus into a moving strip of paper tape, leaving short and long marks. Later, operators used a simpler device called a sounder, which made a sharp click when the armature was pulled down and another click when a spring snapped it back up. Experienced operators learned to hear the rhythm of the clicks and write down the message by ear, so the paper tape was no longer needed.

To turn on-and-off pulses into words, the team needed a code. Each letter got its own pattern of short signals, called dots, and long signals, called dashes. Alfred Vail is believed to have done much of the work of matching letters to patterns. According to a well-known account, he visited a newspaper print shop in Morristown and counted how many pieces of metal type the printers kept for each letter. Printers keep lots of E's and T's because those letters are used most often, and only a few Q's and Z's. So in the code, E became a single dot and T a single dash, while rare letters got longer patterns. This made messages quicker to send.

The code they made, now called American Morse code, had some extra-long dashes and odd spaces inside certain letters. In 1848 a German engineer named Friedrich Gerke simplified it, and in 1865 an international meeting of telegraph countries in Paris agreed on a standard version, International Morse code. That is the version most people learn today, where SOS is three dots, three dashes, three dots. A skilled operator could send and receive dozens of words a minute, tapping out letters so fast that onlookers could not follow.

sections.heading: Inside the Circuit: Battery, Key, Wire, Click
paragraphs: Let's follow a single dot from start to finish, as if we were tiny enough to ride along with the electricity. Our journey starts at a battery in the sending office. In the 1840s this was a row of glass jars filled with acid and metal plates, a descendant of Volta's pile. The battery is always ready to push current, but only if there is a complete loop, called a circuit, for the current to flow around.

The operator presses the key. Two metal contacts touch, and the circuit is complete. Current rushes out along the wire on its poles, travels the whole distance to the receiving office, flows round and round the coil of the electromagnet there, and then goes down into a metal plate buried in the damp earth. The earth itself carries the current back, completing the loop. Using the ground instead of a second return wire was a trick worked out by the German scientist Carl August von Steinheil in 1838, and it cut the cost of building lines nearly in half.

While current flows, the iron core of the far electromagnet becomes a magnet and yanks the armature down: click. The operator releases the key after a short moment, the circuit breaks, the magnetism vanishes, and a spring pulls the armature back up: clack. A short gap between click and clack is a dot. A longer gap is a dash. Silence of different lengths separates letters and words. Everything in the message is just timing.

Over long distances, the current grew weaker because the wire resisted it and some leaked away through damp poles. That is where Joseph Henry's relay idea mattered. At a relay station, the weak incoming current was strong enough only to move a very light switch, but that switch connected a fresh local battery to the next stretch of line. The message was copied, click for click, into a strong new signal and sent onward. By chaining relays, messages could cross hundreds and then thousands of kilometres.

sections.heading: What Hath God Wrought
paragraphs: Building a telegraph line between cities cost far more than Morse could afford. For years he begged Congress for help, and many members laughed at the idea. Finally, on March 3, 1843, the very last day of that session of Congress, a bill was signed giving him 30,000 dollars to build an experimental line from Washington, D.C., to Baltimore, Maryland.

The builders first tried to bury the wire underground inside lead pipes, using a special plough designed by a young man named Ezra Cornell, who later helped found Western Union and Cornell University. But the buried wires leaked electricity and failed, and much of the money was spent. So the team changed plans and hung the wire on wooden poles alongside the Baltimore and Ohio Railroad, with glass and other materials used to keep the current from leaking into the poles. By May 1844 the wire stretched about 60 kilometres (nearly 40 miles) between the two cities.

Even before the official opening, the line proved its worth. On May 1, 1844, the Whig Party met in Baltimore and chose Henry Clay as its candidate for president. Vail, working at a station along the line, sent the news to Morse in Washington, where it arrived about an hour before the train carrying the same news. A few weeks later, people crowded around the telegraph to follow live updates from the Democratic convention in Baltimore.

The famous official demonstration came on May 24, 1844. Morse sat at his instrument in the Capitol building in Washington. Annie Ellsworth, the young daughter of the Commissioner of Patents, a friend of Morse, had been allowed to choose the message. She picked a phrase from the Bible, from the Book of Numbers: What hath God wrought. In plain modern English it means something like: look at what God has done. Morse tapped out the dots and dashes, and in Baltimore Alfred Vail received them and sent the same words straight back. The original paper tape, with Morse's handwritten note about it, is kept today at the Library of Congress.

It was not the first electric telegraph message ever sent, since Britain already had working lines. But it was the first long-distance public demonstration of Morse's system in the United States, and it convinced Americans that the telegraph worked.

sections.heading: Wires Across a Continent
paragraphs: After 1844, telegraph lines spread across the United States astonishingly fast. Private companies strung wire between towns, often along railways, roads and rivers. By the early 1850s there were tens of thousands of kilometres of telegraph wire in the country, run by dozens of competing companies. It was messy: some lines were badly built, and messages often had to be handed from one company to another.

Railways became some of the telegraph's best customers. In 1851, a superintendent of the Erie Railroad named Charles Minot began using telegraph messages to direct trains, telling them where to wait and when to go. This let a railway run more trains safely on a single track. Newspapers also changed. Instead of waiting days for news from distant cities, editors could print stories that had happened the day before. In 1846, several New York newspapers began sharing the cost of sending news by telegraph, an early step toward the news organisation later called the Associated Press.

A message sent by telegraph and delivered on paper was called a telegram. You walked into a telegraph office, wrote your message on a form, and paid by the word. Because every word cost money, people learned to write in a very short, clipped style, such as ARRIVING TUESDAY NOON STOP SEND CARRIAGE. A messenger, often a teenage boy, then ran or cycled the telegram from the receiving office to the person's door. Telegraph operating became a respected skilled job. A woman named Sarah Bagley is often named as the first American woman telegraph operator, in Lowell, Massachusetts, in 1846. A young Thomas Edison, who later improved the telephone, worked as a travelling telegraph operator as a teenager.

In 1856 several companies combined to form the Western Union Telegraph Company, led by Hiram Sibley, and it soon became one of the largest companies in America. When Congress passed the Pacific Telegraph Act in 1860, offering support for a line from the Missouri River to California, Western Union took on the job. Crews began in two directions. Edward Creighton led a team building westward from Nebraska and put up his first pole on July 4, 1861, while another crew built eastward from California. They faced deserts, mountains, freezing weather and the problem of finding wooden poles where few trees grew.

The two lines met in Salt Lake City, and the first transcontinental telegraph was completed on October 24, 1861. Among the first messages was one from California to President Abraham Lincoln, sent by Stephen Field, the Chief Justice of California, promising that California would stay loyal to the Union as the Civil War began. Just two days later, the famous Pony Express, whose young riders had galloped mail across the West in about ten days, announced that it was closing. A rider could never compete with a message that crossed the continent in minutes. During the Civil War, Lincoln spent hours in the War Department's telegraph office reading reports from his generals, making him one of the first leaders to follow a war almost as it happened.

sections.heading: Amazing, But Not Yet a Voice
paragraphs: The electric telegraph was one of the biggest changes in human history. For the first time, information could travel far faster than any person, animal or vehicle. Prices in one city could be known in another the same hour. Families could hear about a birth or a death in a day instead of weeks. Governments, armies, railways and businesses all started to depend on it.

But it had limits. Ordinary people could not use a telegraph themselves. You needed a trained operator who knew the code and could tap it out quickly and accurately. You had to go to a telegraph office, which might be miles away, and pay by the word. Messages were short and often stiff, like little notes in a hurry. And no matter how fast the operator tapped, the telegraph could only carry clicks. You could not hear your mother laugh, your friend's excitement or the worried tone in someone's voice.

There were arguments, too. Morse fought long court battles to defend his patent against rival telegraph makers. In 1853 the US Supreme Court, in a case called O'Reilly v. Morse, agreed that Morse's own system was his invention, but ruled that he could not claim to own every possible use of electromagnetism for sending signals at a distance. In Britain, Cooke and Wheatstone quarrelled so badly over credit that a special panel had to give its opinion, which praised both men. Arguments over who invented what would come back even louder with the telephone.

Each wire could also carry only one message at a time, so busy lines became crowded. Inventors began wondering whether a single wire could carry several messages at once, perhaps using different musical tones. That puzzle, as we will see later, would lead some of them straight toward the telephone.

There was one more giant problem. Wires could be hung on poles across fields, forests, deserts and mountains. But what about the sea? Between Britain and France lay the stormy English Channel, and between Europe and America lay the vast, deep Atlantic Ocean. Ships still took about ten days to carry news across it. To truly connect the world, someone would have to lay a wire along the bottom of the ocean.

deepDive: Historians increasingly describe the electric telegraph as a case of simultaneous invention rather than the work of one genius. Schilling in Russia, Gauss and Weber in Göttingen, Steinheil in Munich, Cooke and Wheatstone in London and Morse and Vail in the United States all built working systems within roughly a decade, because the same scientific ingredients had become available to all of them: Volta's battery (1800), Ørsted's discovery that current deflects a magnetic needle (1820), and the powerful multi-turn electromagnets developed by Joseph Henry and others around 1830. What separated the systems was engineering and economics. The Cooke and Wheatstone five-needle design could be read by an untrained clerk but needed five or six wires; Morse's design needed only one wire plus an earth return, at the price of requiring trained operators who knew the code. In the long run, the cheaper single wire won almost everywhere, and even British railways moved toward single-needle and Morse equipment. Morse code itself is an early example of efficient coding: by giving the most frequent letters (E, T) the shortest signals, it reduced average transmission time, an idea that information theorists such as Claude Shannon later made mathematically precise. Credit within the American team is still discussed. Morse held the patents and the fame, but many historians believe Alfred Vail contributed much of the mechanical design and the dot-dash alphabet, and Joseph Henry's research on electromagnets and relays made long lines possible; Henry later felt Morse did not acknowledge this fairly. The economic effects were enormous. The telegraph separated communication from transportation for the first time, allowing prices for goods such as cotton and grain to converge between distant markets, letting railways schedule trains safely on single tracks, and supporting the rise of large national companies such as Western Union, which by the late 1860s dominated American telegraphy. Its weakness was that it needed skilled intermediaries, which kept it a service people visited rather than a device they owned.
funFact: Because Cooke and Wheatstone's needle telegraph had no letter Q, the 1845 message that led to the capture of the murderer John Tawell had to describe him as dressed like a 'KWAKER'.
